abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Both fruquintinib and TAS‐102 monotherapies are guideline‐recommended for third‐line treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC). This study aimed to analyze the preliminary outcomes of fruquintinib combined with TAS‐102, with or without stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), as a third‐ or later‐line therapy for mCRC. This prospective, two‐arm, phase II study planned to enroll 66 patients with mCRC who were unresponsive to at least two prior lines of therapy. Patients were allocated to either the FTS (fruquintinib + TAS‐102 + SBRT) or FT (fruquintinib + TAS‐102) group. Eligible patients received fruquintinib (4 mg, qd, days 1–21) and TAS‐102 (30 mg/m2, bid, days 1–5; 15–19) orally every 4 weeks until disease progression or intolerable toxicity. The primary endpoint was progression‐free survival (PFS, per RECIST 1.1); secondary endpoints included overall survival (OS), objective response rate (ORR), disease control rate (DCR), and adverse events (AEs, graded using CTCAE v5.0). By January 20, 2025, 40 patients were enrolled (FTS group, 11; FT group, 29), with a median follow‐up of 8.48 months. In 20 (50%) patients, the number of metastatic organs was ≥ 3. However, the number of metastatic lesions was > 5 in 32 (80%) patients. For the 36 eligible patients, the ORR and DCR were 19.4% and 88.9%, respectively. The median PFS was 8.58 months; however, the median OS has not been attained. The most common treatment‐related AE was decreased white blood cell count (92.5%); grade 3–4 AEs included decreased lymphocyte count (12.5%). No treatment‐related death occurred. Fruquintinib combined with TAS‐102, with or without SBRT, showed promising preliminary efficacy and acceptable safety as third‐ or later‐line treatment of mCRC.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is among the most common malignant tumors worldwide, ranking third in incidence and second in mortality among all cancers [1]. Despite breakthroughs and advancements in the systemic treatment of metastatic CRC (mCRC), the curative effect after the failure of second‐line treatment remains limited. Currently, only three drugs are recommended in the guidelines for the third‐line treatment of mCRC; however, the curative effect of monotherapy with these drugs is often unsatisfactory. Moreover, the median progression‐free survival (mPFS) of monotherapy with the third‐line treatment drugs—Regorafenib [2], Fruquintinib [3] or Trifluridine/Tipiracil (TAS‐102) [4]—does not exceed 3.7 months, and their improvement of mPFS compared with a placebo group is limited. Consequently, the median overall survival (mOS) is < 10 months, highlighting the urgent need to explore new treatment regimens to improve survival outcomes in third‐line and subsequent treatment lines. The SUNLIGHT study, reported in 2023, combined TAS‐102 and bevacizumab as third‐line treatment, yielding a mPFS of 5.6 months and a mOS of 10.8 months, demonstrating good efficacy and promising prospects [5]. This finding suggests that the combination of targeted anti‐angiogenic drugs and TAS‐102 might offer a superior alternative to monotherapy for third‐line treatment of patients with advanced CRC, potentially improving survival outcomes.

Fruquintinib is a quinazoline‐based, small‐molecule angiogenesis inhibitor. It primarily targets and inhibits the Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor Receptor (VEGFR) kinase family (VEGFR1, 2, and 3), thereby limiting the formation of new tumor blood vessels and ultimately exerting an inhibitory effect on tumor growth [6]. TAS‐102 is a cytotoxic antitumor drug composed of the thymidine analogs trifluridine (FTD) and the thymidine phosphorylase inhibitor, tipiracil hydrochloride. Its main mechanism of action involves the substitution of thymine with FTD, which is incorporated into the DNA double helix during replication, leading to DNA dysfunction and subsequent antitumor effect [7]. In several studies on the combination of TAS‐102 and bevacizumab for third‐line treatment of mCRC, the mPFS was approximately 4.6 months at most, whereas the mOS was 10.86 months [8, 9]. Moreover, the effectiveness of the biweekly regimen was not inferior to that of the 4‐week regimen, and its safety profile was preferable. Basic research has confirmed the feasibility of the combined use of fruquintinib and TAS‐102 through in vitro experiments. The results indicated that fruquintinib enhances the DNA‐damaging effect of TAS‐102, creating a synergistic antitumor effect [10].

Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) is a core component of the local treatment of malignant tumors [11], with a high efficacy and safety profile. For patients with mCRC complicated by metastasis to the liver, lungs, and other sites, SBRT can increase the local tumor control rate and prolong PFS. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that TAS‐102 impairs DNA damage repair following radiotherapy by inhibiting thymidylate synthase. Moreover, combining radiotherapy with other treatments can significantly increase the proportion of cells in the DNA sequencing phase, thus enhancing the damaging effect of radiotherapy on DNA replication stress [12]. VEGFR inhibitors can reverse the radio‐resistance of tumor cells by pruning abnormal tumor blood vessels, improving blood flow perfusion and oxygenation [13], and alleviating tumor hypoxia. Further, both chemotherapy and anti‐angiogenic targeted therapy can enhance radiosensitivity, providing a theoretical basis for combined treatment regimens of these three treatment methods.

Presently, prospective studies on the overall strategy of using SBRT as a third‐line and subsequent treatment approach for mCRC are limited. Consequently, the optimal regimen for combining targeted therapy, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy remains unclear. This novel prospective study aimed to evaluate the preliminary efficacy and safety of integrating fruquintinib and TAS‐102 with or without SBRT for third‐line and subsequent treatment of mCRC.

sec.title: Study Population
sec.p: This prospective, two‐arm, Phase II clinical trial recruited patients with mCRC aged > 18 years, histologically diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, who had progressed after standard first‐ and second‐line treatments. Other inclusion criteria included good compliance, voluntary participation, signing of the informed consent form, an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status (ECOG‐PS) score of 0–2, at least one measurable lesion, and routine blood and biochemical tests indicating normal organ function (according to the response evaluation criteria in solid tumors [RECIST] 1.1 standard). Exclusion criteria were the presence of other primary tumors; active bleeding or thrombotic events within 3 months; poorly controlled medical conditions such as uncontrollable hypertension, heart disease, decompensated liver cirrhosis, and renal failure requiring dialysis treatment; and a history of allergy to fruquintinib or TAS‐102. This study was reviewed and obtained approval from the Ethics Committee of the Ningbo No. 2 Hospital (No. YJ‐NBEY‐KY‐2023‐025‐05). This study was also registered on the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry website (no. ChiCTR2300070877). All patients received treatment according to the protocol after signing a written informed consent form.

sec.title: Study Procedures
sec.p: Upon enrollment, the research team determined whether SBRT was suitable for each patient. The patients were subsequently assigned to either cohort 1 (FTS group: fruquintinib + TAS‐102 + SBRT) or cohort 2 (FT group: fruquintinib + TAS‐102). The specific treatment and administration regimen were as follows: Fruquintinib 4 mg, orally, once daily, from days 1–21, every 4 weeks; TAS‐102 30 mg/m [2] twice daily, orally, from days 1–5 and days 15–19, every 4 weeks; the research team selected suitable tumor lesions for SBRT, with a dose of 5–10 Gy × 5 fractions, continuously irradiated daily, and completed within 1 week. The principles of implementing radiotherapy refer to the recommendations of the ESMO guidelines, especially suitable for patients with oligometastasis or oligoprogression; general principles for a finite dose for vital organs are documented in a report by Timmerman [14]. Radiotherapy doses for common metastatic sites were as follows: 35 Gy in five fractions for central lung lesions; 50 Gy in five fractions for peripheral lung lesions; 25 Gy in five fractions for posterior peritoneal lesions; and 40 Gy in five fractions for liver lesions. The above combined treatment has a cycle of every 4 weeks until disease progression or intolerable treatment toxicity occurs.

Both Fruquintinib and TAS‐102 were adjusted within the established range. In the event of a treatment‐related adverse event (AE), the research doctor decided whether to postpone or terminate the treatment.

sec.title: Follow‐Up
sec.p: The study had a 28‐day screening period before treatment began. During this period, baseline laboratory tests and examinations were completed, and the imaging data of the target lesions at baseline were captured. Imaging examinations were conducted every 8 weeks after treatment initiation, and the treatment response was evaluated according to the RECIST 1.1 standard. Routine laboratory tests, including blood, urine, stool, biochemistry, coagulation function, thyroid function, and electrocardiogram examinations, were performed every 3 weeks.

AEs were recorded throughout the study treatment. Patients were observed, and relevant information was recorded through telephone follow‐ups, outpatient visits, or inpatient records, with follow‐ups conducted every 4 weeks.

sec.title: Endpoints and Evaluation Criteria
sec.p: The standard for evaluating effectiveness: The RECIST 1.1 standard was adopted to determine the disease status.

The standard for evaluating safety: AE severity was graded according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) v5.0 standard of the National Cancer Institute (NCI) of the United States. During the study period, AEs were accurately documented in the record form, including the time of first occurrence, severity grade, correlation with the study treatment, duration, treatment measures taken, and prognosis performance.

The primary endpoint was PFS, which refers to the time from treatment initiation to the first reported disease progression or death from any cause. Secondary endpoints included OS: objective response rate (ORR), which is the percentage of patients achieving complete response (CR) or partial response (PR); disease control rate (DCR), which is the percentage of patients achieving CR, PR, or stable disease (SD); duration of response (DoR); quality of life scores; and adverse reactions.

sec.title: Sample Size Calculation
sec.p: This single‐center, two‐arm study planned to enroll 66 patients. Sample size estimation was necessary to validate treatment efficacy. The number of events for the primary endpoint of PFS was based on the following assumptions [1]: a two‐sided significance level of 0.05 [2]; a test power of 80%; and [3] an expected median PFS of 5.6 months (based on the SUNLIGHT study, which showed an mPFS of 5.6 months with a combination of bevacizumab and TAS‐102). Following a 12‐month enrollment period and a 10‐month follow‐up, 57 patients were required. However, considering a dropout rate of 15%, 66 patients were ultimately required, comprising 33 patients each in Cohorts 1 and 2.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: For data analysis, the SPSS 15.0 statistical software was used. The Kaplan–Meier method was used to calculate PFS, OS, and their 95% confidence intervals (CI); afterward, a survival curve was drawn. A p value < 0.05 was considered significant.
The ORR and DCR were calculated using RECIST v1.1. AEs were analyzed descriptively according to the NCI‐CTCAE v5.0.

sec.title: Baseline Characteristics
sec.p: As of January 20, 2025, 42 patients had signed the informed consent form. Following screening, one patient was disqualified due to liver insufficiency and did not receive treatment. Another patient withdrew from the study in advance due to poor compliance and treatment refusal. Consequently, only 40 patients were included and prospectively analyzed (Figure 1). Notably, 11 and 29 patients were in the FTS and FT groups, respectively. The baseline characteristics at the time of enrollment are presented in Table 1. The median age was 63.5 years (range: 26–76 years). The primary tumor was located on the left side in 27 (67.5%) patients. In 20 (50%) patients, the number of metastatic organs was ≥ 3. However, the number of metastatic lesions was > 5 in 32 (80%) patients. Liver and lung metastases were each observed in 25 (62.5%) patients. In 30 (75%) patients, the number of previous treatment lines was ≥ 3.16 (40%) patients had previously received fruquintinib, while 29 (72.5%) had previously received bevacizumab treatment. KRAS mutant type was observed in 23 (57.5%) patients, and only one case (2.5%) was of the BRAF mutant type. All patients were of the MSS/pMMR type.

sec.title: Efficacy Analysis
sec.p: A total of 40 patients were included in this study, with 11 and 29 patients in the FTS and FT groups, respectively. Of these, 36 patients received at least one post‐baseline tumor assessment. During the research, 23 (63.89%) patients had reduced target lesion burden compared with that at baseline (Figure 2). For three patients, PFS had exceeded 10 months, and the longest PFS was 17.9 months (Figure 3). Overall, the ORR, DCR, and mPFS were 19.4% (95% CI: 8.2%–36.0%), 88.9% (95% CI: 74.7%–95.6%), and 8.58 months (95% CI: 5.92–9.00), respectively (Figure 4A); however, the mOS was not attained (Figure 4B). When comparing the two groups, the ORR of the FTS and FT groups was 36.4% (95% CI: 10.9%–69.2%) and 12% (95% CI: 2.5%–31.2%), respectively, whereas the DCR was 90.9% (95% CI: 58.7%–99.8%) and 88% (95% CI: 68.8%–97.5%) respectively; although the mPFS of the FTS group was not attained, that of the FT group was 8.58 months (95% CI: 4.57–9.00) (Figure 4C).

sec.p: Notably, patients without prior bevacizumab treatment demonstrated significantly longer mPFS (not reached vs. 7.59 months [95% CI: 4.04–9.0], p = 0.03), with a significant difference (Figure 4D). The mPFS for patients with and without liver metastasis was 9.00 (95% CI: 4.57–9.00) and 7.59 months (95% CI: 4.04–7.59), respectively (p = 0.83) (Figure 4E). In addition, the mPFS for patients with lung metastasis was 8.58 months (95% CI: 5.92–9.00); conversely, the mPFS for those without lung metastasis was not attained (p = 0.80) (Figure 4F). The mPFS for patients with a number of previous treatment lines ≥ 3 was only 6.38 months (95% CI: 4.14–9.00); however, the mPFS for patients who had only received two lines of treatment was not attained (p = 0.11) (Figure 4G). Further, the mPFS for patients who had received small‐molecule anti‐angiogenic drug treatment was 6.38 months (95% CI: 2.66–9.00), whereas that for those who had not received the treatment was not attained (p = 0.18) (Figure 4H). Notably, no significant difference was observed in the survival outcomes of the above clinical characteristics.

sec.title: Safety Analysis
sec.p: The most common treatment‐related AEs were hematological toxicities. The three most common were decreased white blood cell (92.5%), lymphocyte (92.5%), and neutrophil (85%) counts. There were 2 cases of hepatic function abnormalities in the FTS group, considered to be related to radiotherapy. The grade 3–4 AEs included decreased lymphocyte (12.5%), white blood cell (5%), and neutrophil (5%) counts. Two cases of grade 3–4 AEs related to fruquintinib were observed, including hypertension and proteinuria. No treatment‐related death occurred (Table 2).

sec.p: In terms of dose adjustments due to adverse events, 17 patients underwent dose reductions of either fruquintinib or TAS‐102, resulting in treatment discontinuation of fruquintinib in 3 cases and TAS‐102 in 5 cases.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This prospective, two‐arm, phase II clinical trial is the first to combine fruquintinib with TAS‐102 with or without SBRT and is currently ongoing. The existing data shows that the ORR, DCR, and mPFS of the overall population were 19.4% (95% CI: 8.2%–36.0%), 88.9% (95% CI: 74.7%–95.6%), and 8.58 months (95% CI: 5.92–9.00), respectively; however, the mOS has not been attained. The ORR of the FTS group was as high as 36.4% (95% CI: 10.9%–69.2%), and the mPFS has not been reached, indicating that the combination of drugs with SBRT offers a greater treatment benefit potential.

By reviewing the data of classic clinical studies on third‐line treatment of mCRC [2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 15, 16], the effectiveness of monotherapy is less than satisfactory. The results of this study were significantly better than those of the existing standard third‐line single‐agent treatment regimens. We found that the mPFS of patients with the number of previous treatment lines ≥ 3 was only 6.38 months, whereas the mPFS of patients who received only two lines of treatment has not been attained, indicating great potential. Thus, the standard monotherapy regimen for the third‐line treatment of mCRC may not be the best choice, and the combination of TAS‐102 and anti‐angiogenic therapy shows promising prospects. Our findings align with the SUNLIGHT trial [5]. The combination of TAS‐102 and bevacizumab extended mPFS to 5.6 months. However, the mean mPFS in the population previously treated with bevacizumab was only 4.5 months. In a horizontal comparison of survival data, the results of this study numerically outperformed the combination of bevacizumab and TAS‐102. The mPFS of the overall population was not only longer but also reached 7.59 months (95% CI: 4.04–9.0) even for patients previously treated with bevacizumab, which may be attributable to the advantages of the anti‐angiogenic mechanism of fruquintinib [17]. Regarding patients who received treatment with small‐molecule anti‐angiogenic drugs, according to the subgroup analysis, the mPFS was 6.38 months (95% CI: 2.66–9.00). However, the mPFS of patients who did not receive treatment with small‐molecule anti‐angiogenic drugs has not been reached (p = 0.18), indicating that there was no significant difference in survival outcomes between both groups. Thus, even if patients have previously received fruquintinib or regorafenib, they may benefit from the treatment regimen used in this study.

Both domestic and foreign guidelines recommend using local therapy (such as SBRT and ablation) for symptom control or oligoprogressive lesions in the posterior treatment of advanced bowel cancer to achieve the advantages of local control and prolonged survival. This study is the first to integrate SBRT with fruquintinib and TAS‐102, demonstrating a novel synergistic approach that significantly improves tumor regression in patients. Among all patients, the burden of target lesions was reduced in 23 (63.89%) patients compared with that at baseline. The ORR in the FTS and FT groups was 36.4% (4/11) and 12% (3/25), respectively. Notably, one patient had extensive metastases. After treatment, the metastatic lesions disappeared in the advanced stage, and the primary tumor was surgically resected. Eventually, the patient achieved no evidence of disease, which was encouraging. Numerous clinical studies have confirmed that SBRT is a non‐invasive and precise local treatment method that can provide ablative treatment for different metastatic sites, such as the liver, lungs, adrenal, and brain [18, 19, 20]. Previous non‐randomized studies on oligometastases treated with SBRT reported a local control rate as high as 80% and a PFS rate of 2–5 years in approximately 20% of patients [21]. In this study, 50% (20/40) of the enrolled population had ≥ 3 metastatic organs, and 80% (32/40) had > 5 metastatic lesions, which did not meet the criteria for oligometastasis. However, with the addition of SBRT, the ORR of the FTS group significantly increased, although the mPFS has not been reached. With extended follow‐up data, we hope to clarify whether the improvements in ORR can be translated into survival benefits.

A study led by Professor Peng on the dose exploration of the combination of fruquintinib and TAS‐102 adopted a 4‐week regimen of fruquintinib 4 mg combined with TAS‐102 35 mg/m [2]. The latest released data showed that the mPFS was 6.33 months (95% CI: 4.20–8.62), and the ORR was 10.9% [22]. Another study adopted a biweekly regimen of fruquintinib 3 mg on days 1–5 combined with TAS‐102 35 mg/m [2] on days 1–5. The mPFS was 4.44 months (95% CI: 1.99–6.89), and the ORR was 18.4% [23]. Based on the collective experience of our center from a Phase IV clinical research of fruquintinib [24], patients with an initial fruquintinib dose of 4 mg demonstrated the longest OS. The BiTS study showed that the survival outcomes of the biweekly treatment with TAS‐102 combined with bevacizumab were similar to those of the 4‐week regimen; however, hematological toxicity was significantly reduced [9]. Considering the tolerability of post‐line treatment for mCRC, the dose of TAS‐102 was reduced to 30 mg/m [2] in this study using a biweekly regimen to consider both efficacy and adverse effects. Existing results have confirmed that the above drug dosages and administration cycles have a definite curative effect. The mPFS was significantly higher than that reported in similar studies, and the addition of SBRT significantly increased the ORR, playing a synergistic role.

In previous studies investigating fruquintinib‐based regimens for mCRC, hematological toxicities predominated as the primary AEs. For instance, in a 4‐week regimen reported by Peng et al., the incidence of grade 3–4 AEs was 54% (CTCAE v5.0). Conversely, a biweekly dosing strategy adopted in another trial demonstrated improved tolerability, with only 11.5% of grade 3–4 neutropenia. In this study, we administered a biweekly TAS‐102 regimen. Consequently, the decrease in neutrophil count of any grade was 85% (34/40), and the grade 3–4 decrease was as low as 5% (2/40). Notably, most AEs in our cohort were grades 1–2, with the cumulative grade 3–4 AE rate being substantially reduced compared with the historical data. Through the adjustment of drug dosage and optimization of the administration regimen, weekly outpatient follow‐ups and routine blood re‐examination in the early stage of the study were carried out to detect and treat myelosuppression as soon as possible. Investigators need to strengthen patient education during research to ensure that patients can manage adverse reactions well—even when taking drugs at home—which significantly improves medication safety in heavily pretreated mCRC.

This study has some limitations inherent to its design as a two‐arm phase II clinical trial with a limited sample size. First, the preliminary efficacy and safety data remain immature owing to the small cohort (N = 40) and unevenly distributed sample size between the FTS (N = 11) and FT (N = 29) groups, which, without randomization, may have led to selection bias, further affecting the statistical power. Second, the investigator‐initiated decision to administer SBRT introduced a potential selection bias, as patients with an oligometastatic disease status were more likely to be assigned to the FTS group. Furthermore, heterogeneity in SBRT protocols (including radiation dose and treatment timing) limits standardization of the intervention. Third, the analysis relied solely on conventional clinicopathological parameters without incorporating predictive biomarkers (such as genomic or molecular profiling) to stratify therapeutic outcomes, thereby restricting mechanistic insights into inter‐patient variability. To address these limitations, future studies should prioritize phase III randomized controlled trials with adequate power to [1]: validate the incremental benefit of SBRT in combination with fruquintinib/TAS‐102 through stratified randomization [2]; establish evidence‐based criteria for SBRT dose optimization and sequencing relative to systemic therapy; and [3] integrate multi‐omics analyses to identify predictive biomarkers for personalized treatment strategies in advanced mCRC.

In conclusion, this phase II trial provides preliminary evidence that the triple combination of fruquintinib, TAS‐102, and SBRT demonstrates encouraging antitumor activity (mPFS: 8.58 months; ORR: 19.4%) with a manageable safety profile (grade 3–4 AEs: 12.5%) in patients with mCRC. These findings imply that the synergistic integration of anti‐angiogenic therapy, oral chemotherapy, and localized radiotherapy may represent a novel strategy for third‐line treatment of mCRC, though this conclusion is preliminary and requires further validation. If confirmed, this approach could potentially offer meaningful improvements in patient outcomes, underscoring the need for larger trials to explore its clinical applicability and long‐term impact.
